lessons.title: Trace the value behind a pointer
lessons.teaching: A pointer stores an address. *p reads or writes the value at that address. First draw one box per integer, then one arrow per pointer. An assignment through *p changes the box, not the pointer.
lessons.worked_example:
int x=4; int *p=&x; *p += 2;
The arrow still points to x; x is now 6. Write the final value, not the address.
lessons.cue: Address points; star touches the value.
lessons.hint: Draw x and p separately, then apply the compound assignment to x.

questions.prompt: On paper trace: int x=3; int *p=&x; *p += 5; printf("%d", x); What one integer is printed?

checker.solution: p aliases x, so x becomes 3+5=8.
checker.explanation: p aliases x, so x becomes 3+5=8.
checker.feedback: Apply the update to the integer reached by p.

lessons.title: Count allocations and release every owner
lessons.teaching: For an array of n separately allocated strings, allocate the pointer array once, then each string once. Each successful allocation needs one matching free. Release child strings before freeing the array holding their pointers. Strings need one extra byte for \0.
lessons.worked_example: char **a holds 3 separately malloc-allocated strings. There are 4 blocks: 3 strings and the pointer array. Free a[0], a[1], a[2], then a.
lessons.hint: Count the pointer array as one block, then count every separately allocated string.

questions.prompt: A char **names array is malloc-allocated, then 2 name strings are separately malloc-allocated and stored in it. All allocations succeed; no sharing. How many total free calls release every block? Enter one integer; on paper list the freeing order.

checker.solution: 2 string frees, then one pointer-array free: 3 total.
checker.explanation: 2 string frees, then one pointer-array free: 3 total.
checker.feedback: Do not forget the pointer-array allocation.

lessons.title: Unwind a recursive return value
lessons.teaching: Identify the base case before expanding any calls. Write pending arithmetic on separate lines. Reach the base return, then substitute upward. Do not confuse printed output with a return value.
lessons.worked_example: For g(0)=1 and g(n)=2*g(n-1)+1: g(1)=3, g(2)=7. Each pending +1 waits for the smaller call.
lessons.cue: Base first; return values climb back.
lessons.hint: Build a table from g(0) upward; each new row doubles the previous result and adds 1.

questions.prompt:
int g(int n) { if(n==0) return 1; return 2*g(n-1)+1; }
On paper write the calls and unwind g(1). Enter only the returned integer.

checker.solution: g(k)=2^(k+1)-1, so g(1)=3. Verify by successive substitution.
checker.explanation: g(k)=2^(k+1)-1, so g(1)=3. Verify by successive substitution.
checker.feedback: Keep the base value 1 and apply both multiplication and addition on each return.

lessons.title: Splice a node without losing the rest
lessons.teaching: For insertion after p, set newNode->next=p->next before p->next=newNode. This saves the old successor before replacing the edge. For deletion, save the removed node, reconnect the list, then free the removed node.
lessons.worked_example: 4 → 8 → 12. Insert 6 after 4: first new->next points to 8, then 4.next points to new. Result 4 → 6 → 8 → 12.
lessons.hint: The new node belongs immediately after the first node, and every old node keeps its relative order.

questions.prompt: The list is 2 → 7 → 12 → NULL. p is the first node. A new node contains 4. Execute newNode->next=p->next; p->next=newNode. Enter every value from head to tail, separated by spaces.

checker.solution: The order is 2 → 4 → 7 → 12.
checker.explanation: The order is 2 → 4 → 7 → 12.
checker.feedback: Set the new node’s successor to the old successor before redirecting p.

lessons.title: Trace last in, first out
lessons.teaching: A stack pops its most recently pushed remaining value. Keep a vertical column, with the top at the bottom of your written row. Write popped outputs separately so you do not accidentally push them back.
lessons.worked_example: push 2, push 7, pop, push 9, pop, pop produces 7,9,2.
lessons.hint: Cross out only the current top on each pop.

questions.prompt: Start with an empty stack. push(1); push(5); pop(); push(9); pop(); pop(). Enter the THREE popped values in order, separated by spaces. Trace on paper.

checker.solution: The first pop removes 5; the second removes 9; the final pop removes 1.
checker.explanation: The first pop removes 5; the second removes 9; the final pop removes 1.
checker.feedback: Each pop removes the newest remaining item, not the oldest.

lessons.title: Discard the correct half of a sorted interval
lessons.teaching: Binary search keeps an inclusive low..high interval in a sorted array. If key<a[mid], no position at or after mid can match: set high=mid-1. If key>a[mid], set low=mid+1. Recompute mid after every interval change.
lessons.worked_example: low=0, high=8, mid=4. If the key is smaller than a[4], high becomes 3; low remains 0.
lessons.cue: Too small? Search left. Too large? Search right.
lessons.hint: For key<a[mid], remove mid and every larger index: high=mid-1.

questions.prompt: An ascending sorted array is searched with low=0, high=4, mid=2. key<a[mid]. After the standard inclusive-interval update, what is the NEW high index? Enter one integer.

lessons.title: Count work before choosing Big O
lessons.teaching: A loop running n times around another n-iteration loop performs n*n work. A doubling loop takes logarithmically many iterations. Sequential blocks add their costs; nested blocks multiply. Big O keeps the dominant growing term.
lessons.worked_example: A doubling loop followed by a full n-by-n loop costs log n+n², so the total is O(n²).
lessons.cue: Nested multiply; sequential add; dominant term stays.
lessons.hint: Each of the n outer iterations performs all n inner iterations.

questions.prompt: For arbitrary positive n, this code executes work++ in two complete loops: for(i=0;i<n;i++) for(j=0;j<n;j++) work++; Then a separate loop runs 2 times regardless of n. Enter only the tight dominant Big O as O(n^2), O(n), or O(log n).

checker.solution: There are n² increments plus constant work, giving O(n²).
checker.explanation: There are n² increments plus constant work, giving O(n²).
checker.feedback: The two complete n-length nested loops multiply, not add.

lessons.title: Distinguish aliasing from copying
lessons.teaching: An array variable holds a reference. Assigning b=a copies that reference, so both names reach one array. Editing b[0] also changes the value seen through a[0]. Reassigning b to a new array changes only b.
lessons.worked_example: int[] a={2,8}; int[] b=a; b[0]=5; now a[0] is 5. No second array was created.

lessons.hint: Draw a and b as two arrows to the same array.

lessons.title: Choose the outer operation first
lessons.teaching: Before differentiating, name the final operation used to build the expression. Addition splits into separate derivatives. Multiplication of two nonconstant functions calls for the product rule. A function inside another function requires a chain factor.
lessons.worked_example: For (x²+1)(x³-2), the outermost operation is multiplication: product rule first. For (x²+1)^4, the outermost operation is a power of an inner expression: chain rule.
lessons.cue: Name the outside operation before moving the pen.
lessons.hint: The expression is one power applied to an entire inner polynomial.

questions.prompt: For f(x)=(x^2+2)^3, what rule handles the composition? Enter exactly chain, product, or quotient. On paper identify the outer power and inner polynomial.

checker.solution: Chain rule: outer u^3, inner u=x²+2.
checker.explanation: Chain rule: outer u^3, inner u=x²+2.
checker.feedback: A whole expression raised to a power is a composition; include its inner derivative.

lessons.title: Multiply by the inner derivative
lessons.teaching: For [u(x)]^k, first differentiate the outside: k[u(x)]^(k-1). Then multiply by u′(x). Keep the inner expression unchanged until taking its own derivative.
lessons.worked_example: d/dx (3x+1)^2 = 2(3x+1)*3 = 18x+6. The last factor 3 comes from differentiating 3x+1.
lessons.cue: Outside changes; inside stays; multiply inside’s change.
lessons.hint: Use 2*(a*x+b)*a. Both occurrences of a matter.
